cor-bs-interval-consistency.title: Bootstrap intervals are first-order correct
cor-bs-interval-consistency.html: Under the conditions of @thm-bs-residual, the percentile and basic intervals built from the residual bootstrap have coverage probability tending to 1−α.

def-bs-bootstrap.title: Residual and case bootstraps
def-bs-bootstrap.html:
Let X be n×p of rank p, with least squares estimate 𝛃β^ and residuals ε^1,…,ε^n with mean ε^¯.

  1. The residual bootstrap draws ε1∗,…,εn∗ independently and uniformly from the centred residuals ε~i=ε^i−ε^¯, sets 𝛃𝛆Y∗=Xβ^+ε∗, and computes 𝛃β^∗=(X⊤X)−1X⊤Y∗. The design is the same in every resample.

  2. The case bootstrap (or pairs bootstrap) draws n indices I1,…,In independently and uniformly from {1,…,n} and computes the least squares estimate 𝛃β^∗ from the cases (x(Ik),YIk), k=1,…,n. The design changes from resample to resample.

Variants of (a) resample the leverage-adjusted residuals ri=ε^i/1−hii, centred, or the residuals rescaled by n/(n−p).

def-bs-intervals.title: Percentile, basic and studentized intervals
def-bs-intervals.html:
The nominal 1−α bootstrap intervals for θ are:

  1. the percentile interval [q^(α/2), q^(1−α/2)];

  2. the basic interval [2θ^−q^(1−α/2), 2θ^−q^(α/2)];

  3. the studentized (or bootstrap-t) interval [θ^−t^(1−α/2)se, θ^−t^(α/2)se].

def-bs-permutation-test.title: Permutation test
def-bs-permutation-test.html:
Let T:Rn→R be a statistic, large values of which count against the null hypothesis.

  1. The permutation p-value is p(y)=|G|−1#{P∈G:T(Py)≥T(y)}.

  2. The Monte Carlo permutation p-value draws P1,…,PB independently and uniformly from G, independently of Y, and is pB(y)=1+#{b:T(Pby)≥T(y)}B+1.{#eq-bs-mc-p}

The test of level α rejects when the p-value is at most α.

def-bs-schemes.title: Permutation schemes for a partial hypothesis
def-bs-schemes.title_html: Permutation schemes for a partial hypothesis
def-bs-schemes.html:
For a permutation matrix P, each scheme computes a permuted statistic; its p-value is @eq-bs-mc-p with T(y) the observed F(y) and T(Pby) replaced by the scheme’s permuted statistic.

  1. Raw permutation (Manly 1997): F(Py), refitting the full model to permuted responses.

  2. Permuting the regressors of interest (Draper and Stoneman 1966): the F statistic computed from y with model matrix [Z,PX1].

  3. Kennedy’s scheme (Kennedy 1995): regress 𝛆Pε^0 on X~1 alone and compute 𝛆FK(Pε^0), where FK(u)=‖(M−M0)u‖2/q(‖u‖2−‖(M−M0)u‖2)/(n−p).

  4. Freedman–Lane (Freedman and Lane 1983): form 𝛆y∗=M0y+Pε^0, the reduced-model fit plus permuted reduced-model residuals, and compute F(y∗).

  5. ter Braak’s scheme (ter Braak 1992): form 𝛆y∗=My+Pε^, the full-model fit plus permuted full-model residuals, and compute the F statistic for the hypothesis 𝛃𝛃β1=β^1, which is true in the permuted world.

def-bs-wild.title: Wild bootstrap
def-bs-wild.html: Let X have rank p, with least squares estimate 𝛃β^, residuals ε^i and leverages hii<1. Choose transformed residuals ui, one of ui=ε^i,ui=ε^i1−hii,ui=ε^i1−hii, and a law for the multipliers, with mean 0 and variance 1. The wild bootstrap draws v1,…,vn independently from that law, independently of the data, sets 𝛃Yi∗=x(i)⊤β^+uivi,i=1,…,n, and computes 𝛃β^∗=(X⊤X)−1X⊤Y∗. Two standard multiplier laws are the Rademacher law, v=±1 with probability 1/2 each, and Mammen’s two-point law Pr(v=1−52)=5+125,Pr(v=1+52)=5−125.

eq-bs-F-function.html: F(u)=‖(M−M0)u‖2/q‖(I−M)u‖2/(n−p).

eq-bs-case-exact.html: 𝛃𝛃𝛆β^∗−β^=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wε^.

eq-bs-hetero-conditions.html: σni2≥σ―2,Eεni4≤Kfor all n,i.

eq-bs-mc-p.html: pB(y)=1+#{b:T(Pby)≥T(y)}B+1.

eq-bs-no-dominant.html: mn=maxi|ani|‖an‖→0.

eq-bs-partial-model.html: 𝛄𝛃𝛆𝛃Y=Zγ+X1β1+ε,H0:β1=0,

eq-bs-wild-cov.html: 𝛃Cov∗(β^∗)=(X⊤X)−1X⊤U2X(X⊤X)−1,

exm-bs-crime-intervals.title: Intervals for the poverty coefficient
exm-bs-crime-intervals.html:
Return to the state murder rates of @exm-proj-fwl-crime, with the District of Columbia omitted, and the coefficient 0.2538 of poverty in the regression on poverty, single parenthood and urbanization. Seven 95% intervals from B=9999 resamples:

method interval length
t, classical standard error (0.066, 0.442) 0.376
residual bootstrap, percentile (0.064, 0.437) 0.374
residual bootstrap, basic (0.070, 0.444) 0.374
residual bootstrap, studentized (0.071, 0.449) 0.378
residual bootstrap, BCa (0.040, 0.418) 0.378
case bootstrap, percentile (0.080, 0.428) 0.348
wild bootstrap-t, HC2 (0.079, 0.428) 0.348

The residual bootstrap used leverage-adjusted residuals. The first four intervals agree closely: with fifty states and a well-behaved fit, the classical interval is hard to improve on. BCa is shifted down; its bias correction z^0=−0.016 is negligible, but the jackknife acceleration a^=−0.0458 moves both endpoints. The shift comes from that heuristic pairing, not from BCa as such, and opposes the small upward shift of the studentized interval. The case and wild bootstraps give shorter intervals, because the HC2 standard error 0.0869 is smaller than the classical 0.0934 for these data. All seven exclude zero.

exm-bs-engel.title: Engel’s food expenditure
exm-bs-engel.html:
Return to Engel’s data on the income and food expenditure of 235 households (@exm-proj-engel). The least squares slope is 0.4852, and the scatter fans out (Figure 23.1.1(a)): the residual standard deviation is 2.36 times larger for the richer half of the households.

The classical standard error of the slope is 0.01437. The residual bootstrap with B=4000 resamples gives 0.01433, near its exact value 0.01431, the classical value times (n−2)/n=0.9957 (@prp-bs-residual-moments); with leverage-adjusted residuals the exact value is 0.01484. The case bootstrap gives 0.05032, more than three times as large and close to the HC0 value 0.05177 of @prp-bs-case-linear; Chapter 21 computed this and the other sandwich standard errors for the same slope. The residual bootstrap’s answer rests on a constant variance that the data contradict.

exm-bs-engel-wild.title: The wild bootstrap for Engel’s data
exm-bs-engel-wild.title_html: The wild bootstrap for Engel’s data
exm-bs-engel-wild.html:
For the line of @exm-bs-engel, 4000 wild resamples with ui=ε^i give standard errors 0.05119 (Rademacher) and 0.05217 (Mammen), Monte Carlo estimates of the HC0 value 0.05177. With ui=ε^i/(1−hii) they give 0.06653, estimating HC3, 0.06639.

The shape is more interesting. The wild distribution in Figure 23.1.1(b) has two modes, at 0.439 and 0.531. The cause is the richest household, whose leverage 0.255 was examined in Chapter 20 and whose share of the HC3 variance was measured in Chapter 21. Its term ai2ε^i2 accounts for a fraction 0.78 of the HC0 variance ∑jaj2ε^j2, so the condition behind Step 2 of the proof is badly violated. The bootstrap slope is dominated by the contribution aiε^ivi of this one household, which with Rademacher multipliers is ±0.046, and the modes sit at β^1∓0.046. The sampling distribution of the slope is dominated by that household’s error too, and one observation cannot reveal the law it came from; the remedy is the one given in those chapters.

exm-bs-leverage-failure.title: A slope determined by one case
exm-bs-leverage-failure.title_html: A slope determined by one case
exm-bs-leverage-failure.html: Take 15 cases, fourteen with x spread over [0,1] and one at x=4, with leverage 0.902, and a response that puts the far case a little below the line of the others. The least squares slope is 0.254. Without the far case it would be 0.437. In 20000 case-bootstrap resamples, a fraction 0.356 omit the far case, close to (14/15)15=0.355. Figure 23.6.1(a) shows the result. The resamples that contain the far case give slopes tightly concentrated near the full-data value, with standard deviation 0.037. Those that omit it give slopes spread around the fourteen-case value, with standard deviation 0.274. The bootstrap distribution mixes two answers to two questions, and neither its spread nor its percentiles describe the uncertainty of β^1.

exm-bs-stackloss-freedman-lane.title: Acid concentration given air flow and water temperature
exm-bs-stackloss-freedman-lane.title_html: Acid concentration given air flow and water temperature
exm-bs-stackloss-freedman-lane.html: In the full stack loss regression, test whether acid concentration matters once air flow and water temperature are in the model. The F statistic is 0.947 on 1 and 17 degrees of freedom, with p-value 0.344. With 19999 permutations each, the schemes give: raw permutation 0.346, Draper–Stoneman 0.343, Kennedy 0.315, Freedman–Lane 0.345 and ter Braak 0.345. Only Kennedy’s differs noticeably, in the direction @prp-bs-kennedy predicts. The marginal association of @exm-bs-stackloss-permutation disappears once the correlated regressors are in the model.

exm-bs-stackloss-permutation.title: Acid concentration and stack loss
exm-bs-stackloss-permutation.html: Brownlee’s stack loss data (@exm-opt-stackloss-mle) record 21 days of operation of a plant oxidizing ammonia. Regress stack loss on the acid concentration of the absorbing liquid alone. The slope is 0.7590, with t=1.901 and a two-sided t-test p-value of 0.0725. The 5.11×1019 arrangements are too many to enumerate; Monte Carlo with B=19999 permutations gives the p-value 0.0698, with Monte Carlo standard error 0.0018. Figure 23.4.1 shows the permutation distribution of t with the t(19) density. The agreement is close, but the permutation p-value assumes nothing about the error law.

exr-bs-atom-n.title: A1
exr-bs-atom-n.html: Compute 1−(1−1/n)n for n=10 and n=1000. Does the failure of @prp-bs-maximum become less severe with more data?

exr-bs-basic-vs-percentile.title: A1
exr-bs-basic-vs-percentile.html: Show that the percentile and basic intervals coincide when the bootstrap distribution of θ^∗ is symmetric about θ^. With θ^=2, q^(0.025)=1.5 and q^(0.975)=3.5, compute both intervals and explain why they lean in opposite directions.

exr-bs-block-mean.title: A2
exr-bs-block-mean.html: In the moving-block bootstrap with blocks of length ℓ, explain why the bootstrap variance of a sample mean tends to be too small when ℓ is much shorter than the range of dependence, and why a very long block makes the estimate noisy.

exr-bs-case-curved-mean.title: C2
exr-bs-case-curved-mean.html:
Heteroscedasticity is not the only way the residual bootstrap can aim at the wrong variance; a curved mean does it too, with homoscedastic errors. Let X be uniform on {−1,0,1}, let ε be independent of X with mean 0 and variance σ2, and let Y=X2+ε. A line is fitted, so x=(1,X)⊤.

  1. Show that the population projection is 𝛃β∗=(2/3,0)⊤, so U=X2−23+ε, and that Σ=E(xx⊤)=diag(1,23).

  2. Show that Ω=E(U2xx⊤)=diag(29+σ2, 227+23σ2), and deduce that the slope entries of Σ−1ΩΣ−1 and of E(U2)Σ−1 are 16+32σ2 and 13+32σ2.

  3. Using @thm-dep-random-x and @prp-bs-residual-moments(a), identify which of the two numbers the residual bootstrap estimates and which the case bootstrap estimates, and give the ratio of the two standard errors when σ2=0.

  4. Here the residual bootstrap is too wide, the opposite of

    1. Explain why, from where the misfit sits in the design.

exr-bs-case-degenerate-moments.title: C1
exr-bs-case-degenerate-moments.html:
@exr-bs-case-singular shows that a case-bootstrap resample can be one that no least squares fit exists for, when X holds indicators. The difficulty is not confined to indicators. Take simple regression with an intercept and n distinct values x1,…,xn.

  1. Show that a resample gives a design of rank 2 unless all n draws pick the same case, an event of probability n1−n. Evaluate it for n=5.

  2. Deduce that 𝛃Cov∗(β^∗) does not exist as written, and say what a program that reports a case-bootstrap standard error must therefore be computing. Contrast L∗ of @prp-bs-case-linear.

  3. Show that a resample which uses exactly two of the cases, i and j, has slope exactly (yj−yi)/(xj−xi), whatever the multiplicities. Show that the probability of such a resample is (n2)(2n−2)/nn, and evaluate it for n=5.

  4. What does (c) say about the tails of the case-bootstrap distribution of the slope, and which feature of the design controls them? Suggest two repairs.

exr-bs-case-singular.title: B2
exr-bs-case-singular.html: In a one-way layout with g groups of m observations each, find the probability that a case-bootstrap resample omits some group entirely, so that the cell-means model cannot be fitted. Evaluate it for g=5, m=4, and describe a resampling scheme that avoids the problem.

exr-bs-distinct.title: A2
exr-bs-distinct.html: A case-bootstrap resample of size n contains each original case with probability 1−(1−1/n)n. Show that the expected number of distinct cases in a resample is n(1−(1−1/n)n), about 0.632n for large n.

exr-bs-exact-enumeration-perm.title: B1
exr-bs-exact-enumeration-perm.html: For x=(1,2,3,4) and y=(1.2, 0.8, 2.9, 3.1), enumerate all 24 arrangements of y and compute the exact two-sided permutation p-value for the slope. Compare it with the t-test p-value, and explain why the permutation p-value cannot be smaller than 2/24 for any data with n=4 and distinct values.

exr-bs-fl-heteroscedastic.title: C1
exr-bs-fl-heteroscedastic.html: Suppose the errors are independent with variances that depend on X1. Explain why the schemes of @def-bs-schemes need not be asymptotically valid for 𝛃H0:β1=0, and where the argument of @prp-bs-freedman-lane(d) breaks down. Propose a studentized version in the spirit of Section 23.4.

exr-bs-fl-intercept-only.title: A1
exr-bs-fl-intercept-only.html: Show that when Z=1 the Freedman–Lane, Kennedy and raw permutation tests all coincide with the permutation test of Section 23.4.

exr-bs-heteroscedastic-residual.title: B1
exr-bs-heteroscedastic-residual.html: Suppose the errors are independent with variances σi2, and the model has an intercept. Show that the residual bootstrap variance of 𝛃c⊤β^∗ has expectation ‖a‖2n−1∑i(1−hii)σi2, whereas 𝛃Var(c⊤β^)=∑iai2σi2. Construct a two-group example in which the ratio of the two is as small as you like.

exr-bs-iterated.title: C1
exr-bs-iterated.html: The coverage of a bootstrap interval can itself be estimated by a second level of bootstrapping: treat each first-level resample as data, and ask how often its interval covers θ^. Describe how this can be used to recalibrate the nominal level, and count the least squares fits needed with B1=B2=999. How does the design-fixed residual bootstrap reduce the cost?

exr-bs-jackknife-loo.title: B2
exr-bs-jackknife-loo.html: Show that the jackknife values used in the BCa acceleration satisfy θ^(i)=θ^−aiε^i/(1−hii), where a=X(X⊤X)−1c. Deduce that the jackknife variance estimate n−1n∑i(θ^(i)−θ¯(⋅))2 is close to the HC3 variance ∑iai2ε^i2/(1−hii)2. (Chapter 21 shows that the uncentred sum ∑i(θ^(i)−θ^)2 equals it exactly.)

exr-bs-kappa.title: B2
exr-bs-kappa.html: Compute κ2 when Y=ε1+λX2 with X and ε independent standard normals, and the limiting size of the nominal 5% permutation test of zero slope as a function of λ. What happens as λ→∞?

exr-bs-leverage-absent.title: B1
exr-bs-leverage-absent.html: In @exm-bs-leverage-failure, show that the probability that the far case appears at least twice in a resample is 1−(1−1/n)n−(1−1/n)n−1, and evaluate it for n=15. What does a resample with the far case drawn three times estimate?

exr-bs-m-out-of-n.title: C1
exr-bs-m-out-of-n.html: For the uniform maximum of @prp-bs-maximum, show that the m-out-of-n bootstrap with m→∞ and m/n→0 gives Pr∗(Y(m)∗=Y(n))=1−(1−1/n)m→0, and that the bootstrap distribution of m(Y(n)−Y(m)∗)/Y(n) approaches the standard exponential law.

exr-bs-mammen.title: B1
exr-bs-mammen.html: Let v take two values a<0<b. Show that E(v)=0 and E(v2)=1 force ab=−1 and Pr(v=a)=b/(b−a), and that then E(v3)=a+b. Deduce that Mammen’s law of @def-bs-wild is the only two-point law with mean 0, variance 1 and third moment 1, and compute its fourth moment.

exr-bs-no-intercept.title: A1
exr-bs-no-intercept.html: In a regression through the origin, E(Yi)=βxi, the residuals need not sum to zero. Show that if the residual bootstrap resampled the uncentred residuals, then E∗(β^∗)−β^=ε^¯∑ixi/∑ixi2.

exr-bs-percentile-transform.title: B1
exr-bs-percentile-transform.html: Suppose there is a strictly increasing ϕ such that ϕ(θ^)−ϕ(θ) has a continuous distribution K, symmetric about zero and the same for every θ, and suppose the bootstrap reproduces it exactly: ϕ(θ^∗)−ϕ(θ^) has distribution K under Pr∗. Show that the percentile interval has coverage exactly 1−α.

exr-bs-permutation-moments.title: B1
exr-bs-permutation-moments.html: Let v∈Rn be fixed and P a uniformly random permutation matrix. Show that E(Pv)=v¯1 and Cov(Pv)=Svn−1(I−n−111⊤) with Sv=∑i(vi−v¯)2. (The computation is the one in the proof of @prp-dsn-randomization, there for permutations within a block.)

exr-bs-rademacher-exact.title: A1
exr-bs-rademacher-exact.html: With Rademacher multipliers and ui=ε^i, how many distinct wild resamples are there? Show that the bootstrap variance of 𝛃c⊤β^∗ computed by averaging over all of them equals the HC0 variance exactly.

exr-bs-smallest-p.title: A1
exr-bs-smallest-p.html: With B=99 random permutations, what is the smallest possible value of @eq-bs-mc-p? For which α between 0.01 and 0.10 is the size of the Monte Carlo test exactly α when there are no ties (ignoring the chance of drawing the same arrangement twice)?

exr-bs-studentized-limit.title: C1
exr-bs-studentized-limit.html: For independent pairs with Cov(X,Y)=0 and finite fourth moments, show that β^1/se^HC0→N(0,1) in distribution. (Use the central limit theorem for n−1/2∑i(Xi−μX)(Yi−μY) and Slutsky’s lemma.)

exr-bs-terbraak-identity.title: A2
exr-bs-terbraak-identity.html: In ter Braak’s scheme, what is the permuted statistic for P=I? Explain why the observed statistic must still be counted in the numerator and denominator of @eq-bs-mc-p.

exr-bs-wild-cluster.title: C1
exr-bs-wild-cluster.html: Suppose the cases fall into clusters and errors are correlated within clusters but independent between them. Show that the wild bootstrap of @def-bs-wild gives the HC0 covariance, which ignores the correlation. Propose a version in which all cases in a cluster share one multiplier, and show that its bootstrap covariance is the cluster-robust sandwich 𝛆𝛆(X⊤X)−1∑gXg⊤ε^gε^g⊤Xg(X⊤X)−1.

exr-bs-wild-two-sample.title: A2
exr-bs-wild-two-sample.html: Two groups of sizes n1 and n2 are compared through the difference of their means, fitted by least squares with one indicator column per group. Show that the wild bootstrap with ui=ε^i gives the variance σ^12/n1+σ^22/n2, where σ^k2 is the within-group variance with divisor nk, and that ui=ε^i/1−hii gives the Welch variance s12/n1+s22/n2.

lem-bs-conditional-clt.title: A conditional central limit theorem
lem-bs-conditional-clt.html: For each n, given the data Dn, let Un1∗,…,Unn∗ be independent with E∗(Uni∗)=0 and ∑iE∗(Uni∗2)=1. If for every η>0 Ln∗(η)=∑iE∗[Uni∗21{|Uni∗|>η}]→0in probability, then Δn=supx|Pr∗(∑iUni∗≤x)−Φ(x)|→0 in probability.

lem-bs-quantiles.title: Consistent bootstrap quantiles
lem-bs-quantiles.html: Let Rn be random variables with distribution functions Hn, and let H^n be random distribution functions with supx|H^n(x)−Hn(x)|→0 in probability. Suppose Hn(x)→H(x) for every x, where H is continuous and strictly increasing on R. For 0<γ<1, let ξ^n(γ)=inf{x:H^n(x)≥γ} and ξ(γ)=H−1(γ). Then ξ^n(γ)→ξ(γ) in probability, and Pr(Rn≤ξ^n(γ))→γ.

lem-bs-rank.title: Ranks of exchangeable values
lem-bs-rank.html: For real numbers t0,…,tm, let Rj=#{i:ti≥tj}. Then #{j:Rj≤k}≤k for every k. Consequently, if (T0,…,Tm) is an exchangeable random vector and R0=#{i:Ti≥T0}, then Pr(R0≤k)≤k/(m+1).

lem-bs-residual-tails.title: Residuals have uniformly small tails
lem-bs-residual-tails.html: In the setting above, σ^∗2→σ2 in probability, and for every sequence of constants Kn→∞, n−1∑iε~i21{|ε~i|>Kn}→0 in probability.

prp-bs-case-linear.title: The case bootstrap, linearized, is the sandwich
prp-bs-case-linear.title_html: The case bootstrap, linearized, is the sandwich
prp-bs-case-linear.html: Let 𝛆L∗=(X⊤X)−1X⊤Wε^. Then E∗(L∗)=0 and Cov∗(L∗)=(X⊤X)−1(∑iε^i2x(i)x(i)⊤)(X⊤X)−1, the sandwich covariance estimator HC0 of Chapter 21 (@thm-het-sandwich).

prp-bs-freedman-lane.title: The Freedman–Lane scheme
prp-bs-freedman-lane.html:
In the setting above:

  1. 𝛆𝛆F(M0y+Pε^0)=F(Pε^0) for every P, and 𝛆F(y)=F(ε^0). ter Braak’s permuted statistic equals 𝛆F(Pε^).

  2. Under H0, 𝛆𝛆ε^0=(I−M0)ε. The p-values of the Freedman–Lane, ter Braak, Kennedy and Draper–Stoneman schemes depend on y only through (I−M0)y, so under H0 their distributions do not depend on 𝛄γ. The raw permutation statistic involves 𝛄γ.

  3. Under H0, if PZ=Z for every P in a group G and 𝛆ε is G-invariant in distribution, then the Freedman–Lane test over G is exact, and it coincides with the raw permutation test over G.

  4. Suppose the errors are independent draws from one law with mean zero and variance σ2>0, P is uniform over all permutations and independent of 𝛆ε, and p is fixed as n→∞. Then under H0, 𝛆𝛆F(Pε^0)−F(Pε)→0 in probability, and so does 𝛆𝛆F(Pε^)−F(Pε).

prp-bs-invariant-nuisance.title: Permutations that fix the nuisance regressors
prp-bs-invariant-nuisance.title_html: Permutations that fix the nuisance regressors
prp-bs-invariant-nuisance.html: Suppose 𝛆ε is G-invariant in distribution, and PZ=Z for every P∈G. Then under H0 of @eq-bs-partial-model the response Y is G-invariant in distribution, and the permutation test over G with any statistic is exact, whatever the value of 𝛄γ.

prp-bs-kennedy.title: Kennedy’s scheme is anticonservative relative to Freedman–Lane
prp-bs-kennedy.title_html: Kennedy’s scheme is anticonservative relative to Freedman–Lane
prp-bs-kennedy.html: For every permutation P, 𝛆𝛆FK(Pε^0)≤F(Pε^0), with equality when P=I. Consequently, for any set of permutations P1,…,PB, the Kennedy p-value is at most the Freedman–Lane p-value.

prp-bs-maximum.title: The bootstrap of a maximum
prp-bs-maximum.html:
1. n(θ−Y(n))/θ converges in distribution to the standard exponential law.

  2. For every sample with distinct values, the case bootstrap gives Pr∗(Y(n)∗=Y(n))=1−(1−1/n)n→1−e−1.

So the bootstrap distribution of n(Y(n)−Y(n)∗)/Y(n) has an atom at zero of mass at least 1−e−1 for every sample, and it cannot approach the continuous exponential law.

prp-bs-parametric.title: The parametric bootstrap in the normal model
prp-bs-parametric.title_html: The parametric bootstrap in the normal model
prp-bs-parametric.html:
In the normal linear model with rank(X)=p<n, let the parametric bootstrap draw 𝛃Y∗∼Nn(Xβ^,s2I). Then for every data set:

  1. 𝛃𝛃T∗=(c⊤β^∗−c⊤β^)/(s∗‖a‖)∼t(n−p) under Pr∗, so the studentized interval is the t interval of @cor-opt-t, apart from Monte Carlo error;

  2. 𝛃𝛃c⊤β^∗∼N(c⊤β^,s2‖a‖2) under Pr∗, so the percentile and basic intervals are θ^±zα/2s‖a‖, whose coverage is Pr(|T|≤zα/2)<1−α with T∼t(n−p).

prp-bs-residual-moments.title: Moments of the residual bootstrap
prp-bs-residual-moments.html:
In the residual bootstrap, put σ^∗2=n−1∑iε~i2, the variance of the resampled law. Then:

thm-bs-permutation.title: Exactness of permutation tests
thm-bs-permutation.html: If Y is G-invariant in distribution, then for every statistic T, every α∈[0,1] and every B≥1, Pr(p(Y)≤α)≤α,Pr(pB(Y)≤α)≤α.

thm-bs-residual.title: Consistency of the residual bootstrap
thm-bs-residual.html:
In the fixed-design setting above, assume @eq-bs-no-dominant. Let 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃Gn(x)=Pr(cn⊤(β^−β)≤x‖an‖),G^n(x)=Pr∗(cn⊤(β^∗−β^)≤x‖an‖), where 𝛃β^∗ comes from the residual bootstrap. Then:

  1. supx|Gn(x)−Φ(x/σ)|→0;

  2. supx|G^n(x)−Φ(x/σ)|→0 in probability;

  3. supx|G^n(x)−Gn(x)|→0 in probability.

thm-bs-wild-consistency.title: Consistency of the wild bootstrap
thm-bs-wild-consistency.html: Under @eq-bs-no-dominant and @eq-bs-hetero-conditions, let 𝛃β^∗ come from the wild bootstrap with ui=ε^i and multipliers from any fixed law with mean 0 and variance 1, and let Gn and G^n be defined as in @thm-bs-residual, with this 𝛃β^∗. Then supx|G^n(x)−Gn(x)|→0 in probability, and both are uniformly close to Φ(x/τn).
